newsitem.title: USA: Companies find value in warm, fuzzy retro ads.
newsitem.headline: Companies find value in warm, fuzzy retro ads.

text.p: For a number of companies hawking products ranging from cereal to chewing gum, everything old is new again -- at least when it comes to advertising.

Familiar advertising themes and jingles, some mothballed for more than two decades, are making a comeback this year as marketers attempt to cash in on long-established brand equities by conjuring up warm and fuzzy images from the past.

Marketing research is generally the key factor in a company's decision to bring popular advertising themes and jingles out of retirement, said Ken Love, vice president- creative director at Lippincott & Margules, a New York-based brand strategy firm.
Consumers react strongly to the nostalgic images of the past, Love said, adding that such images can work on two levels. "It's nostalgic for the old folks and retro-funky for the kids."

Research was the main reason behind Chicago-based gum- maker Wm. Wrigley Jr. Co.'s decision to bring back the 1960s "Double your pleasure" jingle and multiple sets of twins in new ads for Doublemint gum, said Jennifer Crotty, marketing manager for Doublemint.

"Consumers identify twins with Doublemint and they miss it," said Crotty. Although twins have always been associated with the brand, they have been used sparsely in the ads since the 1970s until they were suspended altogether in 1995.

The new ads, which come out next week, were created by longtime Wrigley agency BBDO Worldwide, New York. The ads begin with the original "Double your pleasure, double your fun" jingle, then move into a more contemporary version of the tune, Crotty said. In addition to the TV commercials, Wrigley also will feature the jingle in radio spots.
"Not only are kids into it, but it's fun for adults because it brings back where you were during your childhood," she said.

Chicago-based Quaker Oats Co. had a similar idea in mind when it launched its "Be the next Mikey" contest for the Life Cereal brand, said Keith Neumann, marketing manager for the brand. "Mikey is unique to the ready-to-eat cereal category," said Neumann. "It's easy to get lost in this category of 200- plus brands. Utilizing Mikey allows us to become top-of-mind again for folks who have forgotten about us."

The original Mikey was the Life-cereal TV spokeskid from the 1970s that amazed his brothers by eating a "good-for-you" cereal. The character was created for Quaker more than 20 years ago by DDB Needham Worldwide, Chicago. The new Mikey, 4-year-old Marli Brianna Hughes of Brandon, Fla., was selected this week from among 35,000 entries. In addition to a $10,000 cash prize, she won the right to be immortalized on a cereal box and the chance to appear in new TV ads for Life beginning in January from Foote Cone & Belding, Chicago.

Resurrecting an old image or jingle also can help transfer a company's brand equity to a new product. For example, in May, when Johnson & Johnson Consumer Products launched a new line of bandages embedded with antibiotics, it brought back the familiar "Stuck on Band-Aid" jingle composed 20 years ago by Barry Manilow.

Although kids may respond to revived ads from the past, companies need to contemporize the images if they want to keep kids' interest, said Arlyn Brenner, vice president in the child research services division of McCollum Spielman Worldwide, a Great Neck, N.Y.-based market research company. "It needs to have a new twist," Brenner said.
Toostie Roll Industries was looking for that kind of a twist when it decided to update its 27-year-old "How many licks does it take" ad campaign for Tootsie Pops last spring.

The Chicago-based company set its familiar "How many licks does it take to reach the chocolatey, chewy center of a Tootsie Pop?" quandary in a new TV spot that substitutes its familiar owl and turtle characters with a computer-generated skull and dragon.

But the company hasn't parted completely with the owl and turtle spot, which will air once for every eight times the new spot airs. "There are many people who have memories and are very attached to the owl and the turtle," said Ellen Gordon, president and chief operating officer. "We didn't want to let that go."
